title: Corded drills, saws and grinders: safe teardown
summary: Corded drills, circular saws and angle grinders all run on a brushed universal motor. Strip one for the motor and its brushes, the gears, spindle and bearings, the trigger switch and the cord. Unplug it and take the blade or disc off first: they cut even when still.

steps.text: Check whether the tool works before you strip it: a working tool is worth more whole (see notes). Then unplug it and keep the plug where you can see it.
steps.warn: Never open a tool that is still plugged in. The brushes and switch carry full mains voltage.

steps.text: Take off the blade, disc or bit. Press the spindle lock if it has one and undo the bolt or flange nut with the tool's own wrench. With no lock, clamp the tool down and wedge a wooden block against the blade body, well away from the teeth. Check which way it undoes before you force it. Wrap blades in cardboard and tape.
steps.warn: Saw teeth and grinder discs cut even when still, and the wrench can slip. Wear thick gloves and eye protection, never hold a blade with your hand or a rag, and keep your hand out of the wrench's path.

steps.text: If the motor body has two round screw caps on opposite sides, unscrew them and pull out each carbon brush with its spring. Hold a thumb over each cap as you undo it: the spring pushes the brush out. Taking the brushes out first keeps them from chipping when the armature slides out (the 5007NB parts list shows two brush holder caps; see repair_motor_brushes). Brush and commutator dust is fine black carbon that conducts electricity and can irritate eyes and skin: wipe it up damp, don't blow it out, and wear a dust mask (Morgan carbon dust SDS).

Remove the case screws. Many tools use Torx or security Torx; the DeWalt DWD112 drill uses seven TR20 security screws (iFixit DWD112). Lift the case half or the motor housing off slowly and photograph how the parts sit.

Before you touch the switch or its wires, wait at least 5 minutes since you unplugged it. A variable-speed trigger switch can hold capacitors, and one Black & Decker design has one fed from the mains (B&D trigger patent). Discharge every capacitor you can reach, and the switch's two cord-side terminals, with a resistor tool, then measure DC volts there. It must read under 1 V before you touch anything. Never measure first (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
Free the trigger switch. Note which wire goes to which terminal, then unplug or cut the field and brush wires. On some drills the cord and trigger come out together as one part (iFixit DWD112).
Take the gear head off the front of the motor housing. The gears sit in grease: scrape it into a lidded tub to reuse on the same gears.

Pull the armature (the spinning part, with the copper commutator at one end and a cooling fan on it) straight out of the field. On many tools its bearings and fan come out with it (iFixit DWD112, Makita 6408 parts, Makita 5007NB parts).
Lift out the field (the fixed coils in the motor housing). Undo the screws that hold it and keep them with it.

Take the gears and spindle. Grinder: the big bevel gear is normally on the spindle and the small one on the armature shaft. Circular saw: expect a helical gear, a spindle lock and a needle bearing; the 5007NB list shows all three. Drill: the gear set sits between the motor and the chuck (Makita 9557NB parts, Makita 5007NB parts, Makita 6408 parts).
Circular saw: the lower blade guard is pulled shut by a small spring. Let the guard close fully before you unhook the spring with pliers (Makita 5007NB parts).
steps.warn: Small springs flick out hard. Keep your face clear and hold a thumb over the spring as it comes free.

steps.text: Pull bearings only if you need them: use a puller, or support the inner ring and press the shaft out. Read the number on each bearing's shield and write it on its bag.

Test the motor (see test_motor): with the brushes back in, measure resistance across the two motor leads and turn the armature slowly by hand. Then check that no lead reads to the metal frame or the gear housing.

notes:
## Before you strip it

A dead corded tool may only need new brushes or a new cord. Brushes are the first thing to check and are quick to replace (see repair_motor_brushes). A working drill or grinder will do more for a workshop than its parts will.

## What's worth keeping and why

- **Universal motor.** The field coils are wired in series with the armature through carbon brushes, so it runs on AC or DC (DOE motors). It is small, strong and fast; the drawback is that the brushes and commutator wear (DOE motors). No-load speeds on the logged Makita tools are 0–2,500 rpm at the drill chuck (Makita catalogue 6408K), 5,800 rpm at the saw blade (Makita catalogue 5007NB) and 10,000 rpm at the grinder disc (Makita catalogue 9557PB). Use it where mains or a generator is available: a blower, a polisher, a sander, a small grinder. A plug-in router speed control slows a universal motor (see build_brake_drum_forge); a lamp dimmer is rated for lamps, so check its rating before you put a motor on it. It is not a generator: with no magnets, spinning it gives almost nothing (see test_motor).
- **Carbon brushes.** Keep every spare set; spares are often taped inside tool cases (see repair_motor_brushes). The logged Makitas use brush sets CB-407 (6408 drill), CB-154 (5007NB saw) and CB-325 (9557 grinder) (Makita 6408 parts, Makita 5007NB parts, Makita 9557NB parts).
- **Trigger switch.** A heavy-duty mains switch. In variable-speed tools it also holds the speed control: one Black & Decker design uses a triac whose firing is set by a potentiometer that moves with the trigger (B&D trigger patent). No source gives its current rating: read the markings on the switch and stay inside them, and use it only with a universal motor.
- **Gears.** A grinder head is a ready-made right-angle drive: the 9557NB list names a spiral bevel gear 10 and a spiral bevel gear 37, which look like tooth counts and would give about 3.7 to 1 (Makita 9557NB parts). The 5007NB list names a helical gear 39 (Makita 5007NB parts).
- **Spindles and bearings.** Bearing numbers are standard, so a 608 from a saw replaces a 608 from anything. Logged examples: 608DDW, 6201LLB, 6202LLB and a 1010 needle bearing in the 5007NB saw; 626Z and two 627Z in the 6408 drill; 607LLB, 629LLB, 696ZZ and 6201DDW in the 9557NB grinder (Makita 5007NB parts, Makita 6408 parts, Makita 9557NB parts).
- **Cooling fan** on the armature, and the **retaining rings (circlips)** and screws.
- **Cord.** 2.5 m on the 6408 drill and 5007NB saw, 4.0 m on the 9557NB grinder (Makita 6408 parts, Makita 5007NB parts, Makita 9557NB parts). Good for extension leads and repairs (see repair_extension_cord).

## Variations

- **Makita 6408 drill:** 3/8 in keyless, variable speed, reversing; the 6408K is rated 4.9 A at 120 V (Makita catalogue 6408K). Its parts list has two brush holders (Makita 6408 parts).
- **Makita 5007NB circular saw:** 7-1/4 in (185 mm), AC/DC, 15.0 A at 120 V (Makita catalogue 5007NB). Brush holder caps, a spindle lock, and a tension spring for the guard (Makita 5007NB parts).
- **Makita 9557PB grinder:** 4-1/2 in (115 mm), AC/DC, 7.5 A at 120 V, two-stage paddle switch (Makita catalogue 9557PB).
- **DeWalt DWD112 drill:** brushes inside the case, and the cord and trigger are one assembly (iFixit DWD112).
- Some newer tools may use brushless motors with a control board; the DOE report says only that the market is moving away from universal motors toward inverter-driven ones (DOE motors). Keep such a motor with its board.
- Part numbers change between versions of the same model: the 5007NB list gives different field and blade case numbers for Types 1, 2 and 3 (Makita 5007NB parts). Check the type on the nameplate before matching parts.

## What to leave

- Chipped, cracked or worn grinder discs, discs whose speed rating you can't read, and saw blades with missing teeth. CCOHS says not to use a cracked or damaged wheel and to check the speed marked on the wheel (CCOHS abrasive wheels).
- An armature with burnt windings or a deeply grooved or burnt commutator: it needs a lathe or a rewind (see repair_motor_brushes).
- Cracked plastic housings, unless you need the handle.

## Testing what you got out

- **Motor:** see the last step. For a run test, clamp the motor down, fuse the supply, plug it in through an RCD (GFCI) if you have one, and run it briefly with the brushes fitted. Insulate the terminals first, keep hands, hair and loose clothes clear of the fan, and don't touch the motor while it is plugged in (see test_motor). Small blue sparks at the brushes are normal; a ring of orange sparks is not (see repair_motor_brushes).
- **Trigger switch:** on the continuity range, the contacts should close as you pull the trigger.
